summary: This document defines a way to carry call control User-to-User Information (UUI) in SIP, a small piece of data an application attaches when starting a session. It defines a SIP header field for the data and the rules for its use.

eli5.summary: When you call someone, a short note can ride along with the ring. This document says how to attach that note to a SIP call and how to read it.

questions: how to send user-to-user information in sip
what is the sip user-to-user header
how to send uui data in sip
what is the sip uui option tag
subtitle: A new SIP header field, User-to-User, that carries a small opaque blob of application data alongside call setup.

tldr.problem: Contact centers and call centers on the telephone network attach a small piece of user-to-user information (UUI) to calls, and SIP had no standard way to carry it as networks moved from ISDN to SIP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7433 defines a User-to-User header field with purpose, content and encoding parameters, a hex encoding, a uui option tag, and rules for defining UUI packages.
tldr.outcome: SIP user agents can pass UUI data in INVITE and BYE messages, through redirection and referral, and interwork it with ISDN, while proxies stay out of the data.

today: RFC 7433 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2015, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its ISDN interworking package is defined in RFC 7434.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Some applications benefit from sending a small piece of data during session setup. RFC 7433 calls it call control UUI data (User-to-User Information). One application inserts it when starting a session and another application uses it when accepting the session. SIP treats the data as opaque and its function is unrelated to any basic SIP function.

The RFC says UUI is widely used in the Public Switched Telephone Network today for contact centers and call centers, and that related applications are moving from ISDN to SIP. The design meets the use cases and requirements in RFC 6567. The mechanism is a new SIP header field plus a new SIP option tag. Interworking with ISDN is specified separately in RFC 7434.

In most cases the two user agents already agree on what to do with received UUI data. The document lets people define packages that make such understandings explicit.
sections.eli5: Think of a sticky note on an envelope. The post office does not read it, but the person who opens the envelope does. UUI is the sticky note on a SIP call.

sections.title: How the Requirements Are Met
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the requirements of RFC 6567 one by one. The header field can appear in INVITE and BYE requests and responses. For redirection and referral it is included (escaped) in the Contact or Refer-To URI. Proxy forwarding and retargeting do not change header fields, and the header carries the data itself, not a pointer to it.

Support is discoverable with a new option tag, uui, used in Require or Supported, and packages can use SIP feature tags such as sip.uui-isdn or sip.uui-pk1. Only user agents are expected to understand UUI data. Proxies and other intermediaries may remove the header field based on policy.

Carrying at least 129 octets of UUI data is trivial, but the RFC notes that very large UUI data is a bad idea because SIP header fields have traditionally not been large.

Integrity and end-to-end privacy could be met with S/MIME, but the RFC says the lack of S/MIME deployment with SIP means the integrity requirement is, in general, not met. Hop-by-hop TLS covers hop-by-hop security.
sections.eli5: The note can be taken off by a post office if its rules say so, and you can ask in advance whether someone can read these notes. Big notes are a bad idea because the envelopes are small.

sections.title: The User-to-User Header Field
sections.content:
The new header field is User-to-User. Its value is UUI data (a token or quoted string) followed by optional parameters. Three parameters are defined:

  • purpose names the package that defines how the data is generated and used. The default is isdn-uui, and if it is absent the ISDN UUI MUST be used.
  • content says what the data actually is. If absent, the package default MUST be used.
  • encoding says how the data is encoded. Only hex is defined here.

UUI data is an opaque series of octets. It MUST NOT be used to convey a URL or URI, because the Call-Info header field already does that. A sender MAY include several User-to-User header fields, and a receiver MUST be prepared to receive several. UAs SHALL ignore UUI data from packages or encodings they do not understand.

For redirection the header is included (escaped) in the Contact URI, and for referral in the Refer-To URI. A UA that supports the specification SHOULD carry such UUI data into the triggered INVITE, much as it does for the Replaces header field in attended transfer. If the target does not support UUI, the header is discarded.
sections.eli5: The note has three little labels: who it is for, what kind of note it is, and what secret alphabet it is written in. If you do not know the labels, you just ignore the note.

sections.title: Hex Encoding
sections.content:
The specification defines one encoding, hex. The data is encoded as base16 according to Section 8 of RFC 4648. The value is normally written as a token, but a quoted-string is permitted, and then the quotes MUST be ignored.

Hex is normally case-insensitive. If a canonical form is needed for a digital signature or integrity check, base16 with all upper case MUST be used.
sections.eli5: Hex writes every byte as two letters or digits, so any data can travel as plain text.

sections.title: Who Inserted the Data
sections.content:
The recipient needs to know which UA inserted the UUI data. Without a History-Info header field, the inserter is assumed to be the source of the SIP message, typically the UA in the From header field or a P-Asserted-Identity header field. In a response it is the UA that generated the response, typically the one in the To header field.

After a redirection, the request may carry History-Info (RFC 7044) with the User-to-User data included in a Targeted-to-URI. If that data matches the request's UUI data, redirection took place, and the inserter is the UA identified by the element before the one that holds the UUI data. In the RFC's example, Alice would otherwise conclude Carol inserted the data, but History-Info shows it was Bob.

UAs supporting the mechanism SHOULD support History-Info and include Supported: histinfo. If a border element such as a proxy or B2BUA removes History-Info containing a User-to-User parameter, the receiver may not be able to identify the source at the SIP level.
sections.eli5: If a note gets passed along, you want to know who really wrote it. The call keeps a trail of who handed it on, so you can tell the writer from the messenger.

sections.title: UUI Packages and Extensibility
sections.content:
A UUI package defines the meaning of UUI data for one application. New packages MUST follow the Standards Action policy of RFC 5226 and be published as a Standards Track RFC. The mechanism is not for arbitrary data. It fits only when, among other conditions, the data is generated and consumed by an application during session setup, UAs are the only generators and consumers, there are no privacy issues, and it is not used for remote procedure calls.

A package MUST define a purpose value, describe the application with use cases, and define or reference a default content value. It may also say which methods carry the data, how many elements are allowed, defaults for content and encoding, and size limits measured on the octet stream. It MAY define a media feature tag. Defining a new option tag only to identify a package is NOT RECOMMENDED.

New content values cannot be added to existing packages, and new encodings cannot be added to existing contents. A new package or content must be defined instead. RFC 7434 is the example package.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note has its own rulebook, called a package. You cannot sneak new rules into an old rulebook. You write a new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UUI data can carry sensitive information. The RFC describes three security models from RFC 6567. In the first, the SIP layer is untrusted and the application protects the data itself with its own integrity or encryption. In the second, the application passes the data unprotected and relies on SIP for security, which is possible in theory but of extremely limited practical use. In the third, a trust domain with perimeter security is used, as in the PSTN and ISDN, with TLS hop by hop and border elements applying policy.

The UUI data in an INVITE can be trusted as much as the INVITE itself. The RFC also notes that the mechanism could be used as a covert communication channel between UAs, conveying information unknown to the SIP network.
sections.eli5: A sticky note can be read by anyone who handles the envelope, so secret things need to be locked up before they go on it.
